title: Early reports suggest record high turnout in Serbia elections
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, People queue outside a polling station in Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city ByNick ThorpeReporting fromBelgra
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, People queue outside a polling station in Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city ByNick ThorpeReporting fromBelgradeEarly reports suggest Serbian voters have turned out in large numbers for the country's election, as a student protest movement attempts to end the rule of its right-wing populist leader.Preliminary reports from the parliamentary election suggest a record high turnout, with 46% having cast their vote by 14:00 local time (13:00 GMT), nearly a million more than the comparable figure for the previous election in December 2023.The apparent high turnout is fuelling the hopes of opposition party Student List that they can oust Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), who have been in power since 2012.The snap elections called by Vučić follow two years of student protests triggered by the 2024 collapse of a train station canopy, which killed 16 and was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia.Anti-corruption movement Student List are running on a manifesto including purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists heading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.Most commentators suggest that a high final turnout, 65% or above, would favour the students.Voting ends at 20:00, with first indications of results expected two hours later. Long queues formed outside polling stations in larger cities and smaller towns alike in Serbia, and at polling stations abroad - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Munich, Los Angeles and Chicago. In Paris, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain.Tensions are high across Serbia. In Belgrade, police have closed streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK).In the street nearby, cars at the traffic lights lowered their windows to blast one of the students' anthems from loudspeakers, 'I want three kisses' - a folk song favoured because the Students' List is number three on the ballot paper. Young people on the pavement nearby started dancing.Image source, ReutersImage caption, People wait in line to cast their votes in capital Belgrade Vučić and his SNS party are number one on the ballot paper. He has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.He retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure.Vučić, who backs Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its war in Ukraine, has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.SNS posters plastered around cities show two hands clasped together in solidarity: the hands of doctors and nurses, farmers, construction workers, teachers and parents. "These are the hands that hold Serbia in their palms," says Vučić in his campaign video. "And with these hands, calmly and with dignity, we shall finish what we started." That is question of this election, continuity or change.Image source, EPAImage caption, SNS candidate Aleksandar Vučić waits in line at a polling station Amid fears of electoral fraud by the SNS, the students have delegated at least two observers to each of Serbia's 8,210 voting stations. Videos circulating on social media on Sunday morning show a cafe in the southern city of Nis, where ballot papers were allegedly filled out in advance in a practice known as 'chain voting'. Signs in the window read "private party". When they realise that they are being filmed, the papers are quickly hidden. There have also been reports of attacks on election monitors and journalists at several polling stations."We are witnessing a unique experiment in European contemporary history," Žarko Korać, a former deputy prime minister and long-term opponent of nationalist parties in Serbia including the SNS, told the BBC. Image source, Guy Delauney/BBCImage caption, Ilija Srdanović tops the Student List's 250 candidates, but would not necessarily lead Serbia if they won Instead of running for office themselves, student-led assemblies at the country's university faculties have chosen 250 candidates to stand in the parliamentary election, with Ilija Srdanović, professor at Novi Sad University, heading the list. The Student List of candidates for parliament also includes doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities"These are people that don't know each other, you have no idea what their political beliefs are, and we now expect them to create a functioning government. So it's anybody's guess what happens after they win," Korać says."On the other hand, if Vučić declares victory this evening, probably late in the evening, I don't think the students will accept that."Korać suggests that many former Vučić loyalists in high office could change sides at the last moment, if the students win. A close result, however, with both sides claiming victory, could result in weeks or months of political instability.The electorate is 6.45 million in a population of 6.53 million, raising concerns about the reliability of the electoral register. Serbs from Kosovo, and dual Serbian citizens from neighbouring Bosnia also have the right to vote.Additional reporting by André Rhoden-Paul

schema.headline: Early reports suggest record high turnout in Serbia elections

title: Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, A man offers residents in Kherson, Ukraine, the use of his Starlink internet after a Russian strikeByTiffany Werth
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, A man offers residents in Kherson, Ukraine, the use of his Starlink internet after a Russian strikeByTiffany WertheimerUpdated 9 hours agoUkraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet.Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network.That vulnerability was highlighted by Musk himself on Saturday, when he accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by using it for "drone strikes to kill people".Saying that loophole was closed last week, he wrote on X, external: "Violation of those terms will result in end of service."He added: "Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately".There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation. France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared with Starlink's 10,000-plus.The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, Iris², however it won't be up and running until 2029.For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death."God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line."For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones.Figure caption, Watch: Who controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?Why does Starlink dominate in Ukraine?Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, are both owned by Musk's SpaceX company and have dominated the global satellite market for years.Ukraine relies on Starlink for communications on the battlefield and Starshield, which is controlled by the US government, for military purposes like drone warfare. The network is able to provide fast, real-time connectivity, which is crucial for defence and intercepting Russian attacks."You can't employ drone warfare without this kind of high-speed internet connection," said Vincent Tourret, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations. Last week's slowdown, which has only just been restored, highlighted the risks of relying on a US provider at a time when tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue to deteriorate."Ukraine's defence cannot depend on Trump's or Musk's whims," French MEP, Christophe Grudler, tweeted.Who authorised the Starlink restrictions is still not clear, with a confusing blame-game ongoing between the Pentagon, Donald Trump and Musk.While Starlink has been one of Ukraine's greatest assets in this conflict, the "flipside of that dependence" has been exposed, explained Kari Bingen, director of the Aerospace Security Project at CSIS."This is a critical military capability that Ukraine relies on, but doesn't control."Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/ Getty ImagesImage caption, Ukrainian soldiers set up a Starlink terminal on the battlefieldStarlink is not the only satellite network Ukraine can access, so if it goes down there are other options - but experts say they aren't as fast, and troops the BBC spoke to agree.Starlink "gives us the upper hand when it comes to passing commands - even one or two seconds are critical when we can transfer data and orders faster, and you can really feel that advantage on the battlefield", a soldier said.The terminals used to connect to the satellites are also an important factor. Starlink's are relatively small and lightweight, so they can be fixed to any kind of vehicle or drone.Eutelsat's terminals "are slightly larger, so they can be fitted on the roof of a car, or on tanks, but they can't necessarily sit on small drones", said Eva Berneke, former CEO of the French satellite company.They are also about five times more expensive, she added.What can the EU offer right now?Rhetoric from the White House - like Trump's scathing criticism of Nato and his threats against Greenland - have given the EU "some pretty brutal alarm bells", Berneke told the BBC. She had only been at Eutelsat for a month when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and said she noticed a marked change in urgency from European authorities, as they looked to her company to help plug holes left by Starlink if it could not be relied upon.Comments from Musk have further heightened the need for an alternative: "Be quiet, small man... there is no substitute for Starlink," he tweeted, external at Poland's foreign minister last year, when the politician said he would "look for other suppliers" if SpaceX was unreliable.Europe has realised its security depends on space, and it must "strengthen its satellite capacities, urgently", a spokesperson for the European Commission told the BBC.Right now, it has Govsatcom, a network that was set up in January to share existing satellites between EU member states. Ukraine is not a full-fledged member (although it is trying to become one), but the Commission is in talks with Kyiv to join Govsatcom.But even if Ukraine could connect tomorrow, the network could not be used for warfare operations like piloting drones, which Starshield is used for.That could change by the start of next year, however, when the European Commission hopes commercial companies, like Eutelsat's OneWeb, will join the programme. This will give Ukraine some - but not all - of its military network needs.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, French President Emmanuel Macron, with a Eutelsat terminal, at the International Paris Air Show last yearEva Berneke told the BBC she is confident the company will be able to "support quite a lot of Ukraine's key military needs". But meeting its communications needs is another thing because, as is the case with most countries, they are varied and massive.Eutelsat could not comment on Govsatcom, but told the BBC that "as the only European operator of a fully operational [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we are committed to providing resilient connectivity to the businesses, governments and communities we serve".No timeline has been given for when Ukraine will be able to join the Govsatcom network. When it does it will likely be as a reliable back-up to Starlink and Starshield.But that's better than nothing, Vincent Tourret said. "If Starlink is shut down, it's good to have another way to stay connected, but it won't be enough for strikes or interceptions, at this stage."Iris² - The EU's future networkGovsatcom is seen as a short-term safety net, until the stronger and more secure network, Iris², external is up and running in 2029.The ambitious project (pronounced Iris squared) is Europe's answer to Starlink and Starshield. It will be a defence-first programme, the European Commission says, with a focus on governments, military and emergency services. Ukraine has been guaranteed access to it from day one.Part of the EU's space programme, the European satellite companies Eutelsat, SES and Hispasat are leading the project in a consortium called SpaceRISE.It will still have far fewer satellites than Starlink, with 348 across low and medium earth orbit - but that shouldn't be seen as a negative, said Kari Bingen."Think about a flash light beaming down - those satellites will be able to cover a greater amount of the Earth, so you need fewer of them," she explained. "They're all trade offs - I would not take it as a negative, that Iris² is planning for less satellites."Tourret was more sceptical: "It's no gamechanger and no great saviour, I'm afraid".Image source, Paul Hennessy/ Getty ImagesImage caption, A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, carrying 56 Starlink satellites, takes off from Cape Canaveral in MarchA highly produced video on the EU Space Policy's website declares: "With Iris², Europe will no longer depend on others for satellite connectivity." So does that mean Ukraine could switch off Starlink? No - that wouldn't be a good idea."Users need to think about communications resilience," Bingen said. "So if something happens to one system, you have other ways to maintain connectivity."It's similar to how mobile phones work, explained Eva Berneke: "If you don't have 5G, you go back to 4G. And if you don't have 4G, you might use 3G, so you have multiple networks for resilience. It's the same idea in warfare."But while a phone might not load pictures as quickly on 3G, for a drone operator, it can be deadly: "That is not a nice situation to have to be in when you're fighting a war."Iris² is not the only option. This week, Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE, external announced they would look at developing satellite communications for Ukraine's military defences. And a joint venture between European satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales, called Project Bromo, is hoped to be another competitor against SpaceX, but it is still in the very early phases.Space projects take a long time, Berneke said, and need "a lot of money". Designing the programme, making the satellites, launching them and then having enough of them in orbit for full coverage takes many years. "Even if you gave me €8bn right now, I don't think I could have anything up there before 2032-2033," she explained.Why Space is the new defence frontierMilitary work in Space is nothing new, and has been happening since the dawn of the space age in the 1950s. But the conflict in Ukraine has shown how integral it is to modern warfare."Communication is so important, and terrestrial communication platforms, whether it's 5G or fibre, can be attacked on the ground," Berneke said. "It is a lot harder to shoot down an entire satellite network. That's not something any military can do right now."While we look to the skies, however, most of the world's communications are travelling via undersea cables - about 99% in fact. But these are vulnerable to attack - this week the UK government outlined new measures to protect its cables, after an increase in suspicious activity by Russian vessels."In a crisis or conflict, there are serious concerns that undersea cables will be cut... so if that happens it's good to have satellite communication as a backup," Kari Bingen said.Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko

schema.headline: Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?

title: Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm
description: ByScotland editorReporting fromRosebank oil fieldUpdated 8 hours agoWhen we landed by helicopter at Rosebank, this oil field was at the centre of a po
body: ByScotland editorReporting fromRosebank oil fieldUpdated 8 hours agoWhen we landed by helicopter at Rosebank, this oil field was at the centre of a political storm - and set to be in the path of a real one.We arrived on Wednesday morning, just a few hours after the UK government had granted consent for the production of gas from the Jackdaw field in the North Sea.But already attention was shifting to this wild and windy patch of the North Atlantic – the next big decision for Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.Rosebank is bigger than Jackdaw, it would generate higher greenhouse gas emissions, and it could be far more lucrative for its owners, Adura and Ithaca.Image caption, Nicola Boyd loves her job on the Petrojarl Rosebank vesselThis summer, along with a camera crew, I travelled to Jackdaw, 150 miles east of Aberdeen.Now we were the first journalists to visit Rosebank.We came here - days before Storm Boelo arrived with strong winds and heavy rain - to scrutinise a controversial project which is at the heart of a national debate about climate change, energy policy and the economy.But we also hoped for a rare glimpse into life offshore."It's good fun, it's interesting, every day can change," said Nicola Boyd, who runs the helideck, and greeted us as we struggled out of our lifejackets and survival suits.Boyd has worked offshore for nearly a decade, including a year on Rosebank - where she spends two weeks at a time followed by three weeks' leave."It's a job I love," she added.Image caption, The Petrojarl Rosebank is moored in the North Atlantic waiting to see if production gets the go-ahead from the UK governmentIt's also a job that calls for steady legs and a strong stomach.Unlike the fixed Jackdaw platform, this installation – 80 miles north west of Shetland – is a large ship, a floating production, storage and offloading vessel (FPSO) named the Petrojarl Rosebank.It's been chartered by the field's owners from Aberdeen-based Altera and, during my 48 hours on board, it was constantly but gently rolling on the North Atlantic swell.Those conditions may be misleading.With the understatement typical of an Orkney islander, lead mechanical technician Ewan Leonard told me the winter weather could be "a bit of a challenge.""Last week we had a 30m heave coming through," he said, referring to the swell, "so we'll probably suffer more of that as the winter goes on."Altera CEO Chris Brett told me that in the industry the environment west of Shetland is considered "as harsh as you get anywhere in the world."Whatever your view on that industry, the sheer scale of what humans have achieved in such conditions is impressive.Image caption, Ewan Leonard says the winter weather can be "a bit of a challenge"The deep reserves of skill, ingenuity and engineering prowess among the 122 people on board are obvious.The jobs are well-paid and, according to Ewan Leonard, the facilities are excellent."We have single-man cabins, there's good gym facilities, there's a lot of rec rooms here."Douglas Hogge, a production supervisor in charge of a team responsible for the safe extraction of oil and gas, agrees."There's the gym, the sauna," he said, adding "you can obviously go and get some fresh air. There's plenty of fresh air out there."There's even a cinema.Image caption, Food on board the ship was described as "fantastic""As you've seen yourself, the food is fantastic on board, so no complaints." added Leonard.Everyone we spoke to agreed with that, praising the talented chefs who sent out all sorts of delicious dishes, from braised ox cheek to mackerel to pork loin, day and night.As dusk gathers and the nightshift get ready for work with a strange breakfast of fillet steak and chocolate brownie pudding, the vessel begins to glow in the gloom.It is a strange sight, the decks criss-crossed by a bewilderingly complex array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelwork.Image caption, The ship is an array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelworkThe ship doesn't move far, rotating around a fixed central point called the turret to face into the weather, making life a little easier for those on board.If production is approved, oil and gas will be pumped up through the turret from wells in the field below, which contains an estimated 300m to 500m barrels, enough for perhaps 25 years."For myself and a lot of the guys, that would see us out to retirement," said Douglas Hogge."We need to see this approved," he added.Environmental campaigners strongly disagree. They've been trying to stop Rosebank for years, with some success."The future of the energy sector in the UK is renewable energy," said Tessa Khan, executive director of the campaigning group Uplift.Consent for production at Rosebank was first granted under the Conservative government in 2023.But in 2025, after a challenge by Greenpeace and Uplift, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled the approvals of the UK's largest known untapped oil field and Jackdaw were unlawful because they had failed to take into account the climate impact of actually burning the fossil fuels in cars, homes and factories.The judge, Lord Ericht, said the fields' developers could carry on with work short of producing oil and gas while they provided more detailed environmental assessments for the government and regulators to consider."We think Rosebank would be a disastrous decision and a terrible deal for ordinary people across this country," said Khan, urging prime minister Andy Burnham to prioritise renewables in his quest to re-industrialise the nation."If the government's interested in building investor confidence, giving the green light to a major new oil field is going to do the opposite," she argued.Whatever happens with Rosebank and Jackdaw, the long-term trend for the industry is clear and it is one of decline.It's a quarter of a century since oil production peaked and in recent years jobs in oil and gas have been disappearing much faster than they're being created in renewable energy such as wind and solar power.The timeline of Jackdaw and RosebankThe oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzle, which looks like the super-sized pump of an enormous floating filling station.From there it would be sold on the international market and, most likely, taken to continental Europe for refining.Opponents say that proves the project is of little benefit to the UK and should be rejected.Supporters argue that's not the case because UK and European energy markets are co-dependent, adding that Rosebank will generate millions in tax for the Treasury.Neil McCulloch, chief executive of Adura – which owns 80% of Rosebank and is a joint venture between Shell and the Norwegian state energy firm, Equinor – is optimistic.He points out that Rosebank contains not just oil but gas which would be piped to Shetland and on to the St Fergus terminal in Aberdeenshire, with the potential to heat 500,000 British homes at peak production.Approval of this project, argues McCulloch, could pave the way for four more Jackdaw-sized gas developments in the waters west of Shetland – Tornado, Tornado East, Tobermory and Suilven."We would like to proceed with them," he said.A surge in fossil fuel production if Rosebank is approved is exactly what campaigners fear.It would, argues Tessa Khan, exacerbate the deadly and damaging impact of climate change for British teachers, nurses, firefighters and families worried about their children while making "huge profits for companies that are already incredibly profitable".Image caption, The oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzleWhen it comes to the impending UK government decision – which sources have told BBC News should come before Christmas – there is a strange mood at Rosebank.The decision in favour of Jackdaw has clearly encouraged many on board but it has also highlighted the jeopardy they are facing.For now, most workers we spoke to said they were just focusing on the job, with its strange rhythms and unusual restrictions – no ability to pop to the shops, no alcohol, a lot of special occasions missed.And for some on board, very particular cravings.For steward Liam Davidson, it is a desire to see his French bulldog, Bailey, at the end of his fortnight on board."My wee dog's at the heliport when I arrive," he said, "I do miss her."Image caption, It is hoped the decision on Rosebank will be made in the next few weeks For Nicola Boyd, it's her double bed and a pizza delivery."I love seeing the family, but for me, it's the pizza," she told me.But this time there might be a delay in delivering Boyd herself.She is coming to the end of her fortnight but, as she helped us into our survival suits, the Met Office issued an amber weather warning for much of Scotland.For Rosebank, it seems, there are stormy seas ahead, one way or the another.Get in touchWhat are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?

schema.headline: Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm

title: The penguins are noisy, the people fantastic - what it takes to be an Antarctic postmaster
description: Image source, UK Antarctic Heritage TrustImage caption, George Clarke is returning for his third stint at Port LockroyByChristopher MaceBristolIt is h
body: Image source, UK Antarctic Heritage TrustImage caption, George Clarke is returning for his third stint at Port LockroyByChristopher MaceBristolIt is hardly a typical round for a postie, but for five months of the year George Clarke leaves behind his partner and friends in Bristol to become a postmaster at the world's most southerly post office - in Antarctica."I thought it sounded like an amazing experience - living away from home for a few months on a very small island with five other people and 1,000 penguins," says Clarke.He takes up his role as Port Lockroy postmaster from late October to March, during the southern hemisphere summer.The part-time festival worker and artist says his days are spent sorting postcards, processing letters and arranging for the post to hitch a ride north on passing ships before being distributed around the world."The penguins are noisy and smelly. The people are fantastic," he said. "I've fallen in love with the Antarctic wilderness."Image source, UKAHTImage caption, Port Lockroy is home to a colony of about 1,000 gentoo penguinsWhen Clarke sets off with in a team of six on Monday, it will be his third voyage to Antarctica helping the UK Antarctic Heritage Trust (UKAHT) to conserve Port Lockroy, a former British science research facility.Unlike a regular post office, there is no fleet of vans ready to whisk the mail away."When we collect up all the postcards and we've sorted through them, we've bagged them up, we've weighed them, we then need to look to see which ships are heading north towards the Falklands," he said."Then we get them on email or the radio and we say, 'Hello, would you mind taking some postcards with you?' And they're always very keen to oblige."Unsurprisingly, running a post office for six people does not take up all of Clarke's time at Port Lockroy.He is also the deputy base commander, helps with the cleaning and maintenance of the site, and helps with wildlife observations for the British Antarctic Survey (BAS)."The primary objective of the charity is conservation of the heritage surrounding UK exploration in Antarctica," Clarke said.Image source, UK Antarctic Heritage TrustImage caption, Postmaster George Clarke says he has fallen in love with the Antarctic wildernessThe team of six is about to embark on the second term of a three-year plan to shore-up and restore the island's largest building, Bransfield House, which is home to a museum, the post office and a shop.They will install beams in the roof and 30 steel and timber props in the floor to help it withstand rain and snow.The site on Goudier Island was chosen in the 1940s to become a permanent British foothold in Antarctica because it was known as a safe place to anchor by early 20th Century whaling ships.The remnants of that industry are still clear to see, with the bones of whales killed long ago for their oil littering part of the shore.Port Lockroy operated until 1962, when British research was moved to larger and more modern sites in Antarctica.Image source, UKAHTImage caption, Clarke (second from left) and the team have been training in the Brecon Beacons before heading to AntarcticaThe journey from the UKAHT base in Cambridgeshire to Port Lockroy takes about a week."We fly to Ushuaia via Buenos Aires in Argentina and we'll probably have a couple of days to acclimatise slightly," Clarke said."We'll then jump on a ship that will take us south to the Antarctic Peninsula and it takes four or five days."Clarke's colleagues are also excited to get the new season under way.Base commander and RAF veteran Carole McCullough said: "I applied for the role looking for a bit of an adventure, and Antarctica is the ultimate adventure."The team work, the bonding, the appreciation of the place - it's all going to make for the most wonderful experience."Wildlife monitor and museum manager Alice Parr added: "I actually applied for a role three years ago and was selected as reserve."I tried again - clearly persistence pays off! I'm incredibly excited to be managing the museum and counting penguins. It's the opportunity of a lifetime."Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: The penguins are noisy, the people fantastic - what it takes to be an Antarctic postmaster

title: Meghan broke contact with father in letter citing abuse claims
description: The Duchess of Sussex broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls, the BBC understands
body: The Duchess of Sussex broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls, the BBC understands.Sources close to the duchess said Meghan warned Thomas Markle in a letter that he would never meet his grandchildren.It is understood the letter was sent to Markle, 82, while he was in hospital in the Philippines after having his leg amputated.It has been reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Markle had been found in his former home in the Philippines and UK police in 2019 told Meghan about claims of abuse against him. Markle, who is based in the US, denies all such allegations. Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. He pulled out of his daughter's royal wedding that year, citing ill health.The letter sent in 2025 appears to be the end of what has been a troubled relationship between father and daughter.It is understood details of the letter, first reported in the Sun on Sunday, external, include Meghan telling Markle that he would never meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lillibet, with Meghan making it clear she would never contact her father again.She also apparently told her father that authorities were aware of the claims made against him.Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed to the Sun on Friday he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home.He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the US Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI) about it in July.The FBI has since confirmed it is aware of the allegations.On Sunday Markle Jnr, 60, apologised to Meghan in an interview with the Sun for initially siding with her father during their long-running estrangement."I now know I have been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years," he said.Philippines officials have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father, telling the BBC on Friday that its anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force was investigating the matter.Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured Thomas Markle's computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.Meanwhile, Thomas Markle has given an interview to the Mail on Sunday, external in which he acknowledged paying for sex in the Philippines on past visits but denies sleeping with underage girls and ever possessing child abuse images.

schema.headline: Meghan broke contact with father in letter citing abuse claims

title: AI in policing risks deepening discrimination, research warns
description: The growing use of AI in policing risks increasing discrimination against minority groups, researchers have warned.Studies suggest that predictions of
body: The growing use of AI in policing risks increasing discrimination against minority groups, researchers have warned.Studies suggest that predictions of future crime hotspots may be based on biased data, which can magnify existing prejudice and create a dangerous feedback loop.Experts are calling for the use of AI in policing to be reviewed with greater human oversight.This would involve checking the data that forces use to find and remove any bias, according to Dr Carolyn McKay, an associate professor and researcher in digital justice at the University of Sydney Law School."The public functions of state policing ought to be subject to human oversight and scrutiny," she says.The problem, according to McKay, is that AI systems are trained on data that already contains human bias, and this can lead to self-fulfilling prophecies.Think of AI as a map-maker asked to draw a map of a city they have never visited. They are locked in a windowless room and can't go outside. All they have are maps that are 50 years old.Anyone following the new map would find themselves stopping at walls that were knocked down years ago and looking for roads that no longer exist. The map-maker hasn't made anything new. They have only copied the old maps.Now suppose the map-maker is handed a list of past crimes and where they took place, and asked to shade in where the next ones are likely to happen. Police then patrol the shaded areas.More crime is recorded there simply because more officers are there to see it. Areas outside the shading appear to have less crime, because fewer people are looking. When the next map is drawn, the same areas are shaded even darker.So the crime figures are not a full list of crimes. They are partly a record of where police have chosen to look.The problem is as old as policing, but AI may be speeding it up.Sarah Brayne, a sociologist at the University of Texas at Austin, spent time inside the Los Angeles Police Department studying how it uses big data. In her research paper, published in the American Sociological Review, she found that the force increasingly used data to predict crime, rather than only to respond to it.She also found that the data fed into these systems was skewed. Crimes in public places were more likely to be seen and recorded, and police focus was disproportionately on black neighbourhoods. Once this goes into the system, she writes, "the predictions appear impartial".The models, she says, create "a feedback loop in which they not only predict events such as crime or police contact, but also contribute to their future occurrence."But that is a view challenged by Dr Dimitrios Kollias, an associate professor in multimodal artificial intelligence at the Queen Mary University of London (QMUL). He says that the technology has moved on to take the bias of historical data into account."The old-map analogy is useful for explaining how historical bias can be inherited, but it has its limits," he told BBC News."Modern AI systems do not simply retrieve or copy their training examples; they can combine learned information in new ways and generate outputs and solutions that were not explicitly present in those examples."But those new insights pose a separate risk, Kollias adds."As AI systems become more capable of generating novel decisions and acting with greater autonomy, we need to ensure that their behaviour remains safe, reliable and under meaningful human control," he said.But arguably a more intractable problem is dealing with the sometimes flawed information stored by authorities and which AI systems draw from. Researchers at New York University said that many of their predictions may rely on what they call "dirty data". These are police records shaped, they say, by corrupt, biased or unlawful practices, including rigged crime figures and arrests of innocent people.In their study, the researchers found that in nine of the 13 US areas they looked at, police data from periods of unlawful or biased policing was available to train these systems.The system can't tell that this data is flawed, according to the researchers. It simply treats it as a pattern to repeat. It is as if the map-maker's compass points only to where crime has been recorded before. The map-maker thinks they have found a new crime hotspot, when all they have done is follow the bias of earlier officers.McKay's answer is to have someone independent check the map before anyone uses it and rub out the lines that are wrong. But cleaning up dirty data won't be easy. The mistakes aren't a few stray pencil marks. The whole map has been drawn on top of them. The New York University researchers say that technical fixes offered by the companies selling these systems aren't enough unless someone independently checks how the data was produced in the first place.Because AI can see the world only through the data it is given, it can make serious mistakes which can harm people. For example, a 2019 study in the journal Science looked at an AI system used in US healthcare to help decide which patients should get extra support. It did this by predicting whose care would cost the most. But there was an inherent bias in the data it drew from. Less was already being spent on black patients than on equally ill white patients, partly because of poorer access to care. By treating higher costs as a sign of greater need, the system unfairly favoured white patients.It was as if the map-maker had been told to mark the sickest parts of the city but had marked the places where the most money was spent instead. When the researchers changed the system to predict how ill patients were, rather than how much their care would cost, the bias largely disappeared. The share of black patients picked for extra help would have risen from about 18% to 47%.Kollias acknowledges that AI bias from dirty data is "an important concern"."But this does not mean that bias is inevitable." he says."We can test systems for unfair outcomes, improve the data and objectives they use, and introduce safeguards to reduce these effects."One improvement would be to provide additional data that provides context. What if the map-maker were given more than a list of crimes? They could also be shown which areas have been neglected - places with broken streetlights, little funding and missing public services. That could show whether the local environment plays a part. Instead of sending police cars to the shaded areas, councils might send money to fix the lighting, support the community and repair the area itself.Yet even this may not be enough, according to McKay."The target environments are still intimately linked with their inhabitants," she says. "They might (continue to) be over-policed and marginalised."She points to systems which were designed to use information about places rather than people. Even so, critics raised concerns that they still led to over-policing.It is as if the map-maker promised to stop writing people's names on the map and to mark only the streets and buildings. But those streets were shaded because of years of neglect and heavy policing, so rubbing out the names changes very little.AI has no beliefs or personality of its own. Like the map-maker in the windowless room, it knows only what it is told. If the person describing the city holds a grudge against one neighbourhood, that grudge ends up on the map.But ultimately the problem is the human bias that fed the AI. People decide what a suspicious person looks like on CCTV, or what counts as a risky loan, and they bring their own cultural, educational and political biases with them. So perhaps AI can be part of the solution rather than a magnifier of the problem, says Kollias."A carefully designed and independently evaluated AI system can make some of these patterns more measurable and visible, giving us an opportunity to identify and reduce them."But humans too have to play their part. The healthcare study shows that those choices can be checked and changed. That is why researchers argue that people must stay in the loop. Otherwise, like a map-maker inking over old pencil lines, AI risks leaving us all in a windowless room, permanently trapped in yesterday's mistakes.

schema.headline: AI in policing risks deepening discrimination, research warns

title: Man Utd captain Bruno Fernandes dropped to bench by manager Michael Carrick
description: Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Sunday's Premier League game against Bournemouth.Fernandes' place in the team has been
body: Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Sunday's Premier League game against Bournemouth.Fernandes' place in the team has been debated since his explosive comments after Wednesday's Champions League humiliation by Como, when he blamed manager Michael Carrick for United's tactics in the 4-1 defeat and his failure to alter them.Carrick refused to say in his media conference on Friday whether Fernandes would be dropped.That has now happened, with the Portugal midfielder left on the bench as United aim to end a seven-match run without a win in all competitions.Asked about the selection on Sky Sports, Carrick called Fernandes' omission "a football decision"."When you have options it's always a difficult decision. We have to make the right one for today and the team to get that performance we want," he added.Harry Maguire takes over as captain, with Mason Mount handed a playmaking role along with Youri Tielemans.It is only the sixth time Fernandes has been left on the bench for a Premier League game. That past two, at the end of the 2024-25 season, were to keep him fresh for important Europa League games.They have won just one of their last 10 Premier League games without Fernandes in the starting XI (D3 L6), beating Newcastle 1-0 in December.Matheus Cunha is also on the bench after being replaced at half-time in Italy, along with Lisandro Martinez, who spoke out about the United hierarchy following the 2-0 defeat at Atletico Madrid this month.Martinez started at Leeds last week but was left out of the Como game because of injury."[He is] not quite [fit enough] - it was touch and go but it wasn't worth the risk."Carrick referred to the Como debacle in his programme notes for Sunday's game."Manchester United is a truly great football club," he said. "Our standards and values have been set out over generations and are very important to me. "As a group, we have a duty to represent you in a manner that is befitting of those principles. "Wednesday's performance was extremely disappointing in many ways. Today we have to show what we are all about. "We all need to stick together but we know that we absolutely have to do better for you. Now, as a group, we need to put in a performance that your support deserves."European football expert Julien Laurens talking on BBC Radio 5 Live: I think if the sanctions against Lisandro Martinez had been the right ones, I'm not sure Bruno would have said that after the Como game.It's about boundaries and having to set limits for your own squad so things like that don't happen and now, for two senior players within the space of six days to go after the sporting director, your owners, your manager, your staff is just embarrassing. It's such a circus.Leave him at home, he doesn't need to be on the bench - it's half of a sanction again. He's just going to be behind Carrick and I don't think he should be there full stop.Former Crystal Palace striker Clinton Morrison on BBC Radio 5 Live: It's a big call but I think it's the right call. A lot of people have raised eyebrows but I do think it's the right call. You can't call out the manager like that tactically.When I was a player, I had a big mouth myself, but one thing I'd do was I'd go toe-to-toe and say it to the manager, or in the changing room or in front of people. I wouldn't go out and say it in the media.But if they don't get a result and you've dropped your best player and your captain, it will fall back on Michael Carrick.No-one is bigger than the football club.Ex-Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher talking to Sky Sports: Bruno Fernandes is Manchester United's best player, we can't get away from that. PFA Player of the Year last year. He had to make the stand, Michael Carrick.Even though he's the best player, there will be a lot of people who don't actually like playing with him in the United team. He's permanently throwing his arms up at people, he's basically saying, 'you're not good enough to play with me'.That's what we see from Fernandes a lot when things aren't going right for United.

schema.headline: Man Utd captain Bruno Fernandes dropped to bench by manager Michael Carrick

title: 'Fostering saved my life,' says Bristol care leaver
description: 'I entered foster care at 14 and it saved my life'Image caption, Amy Burns says she would not be here today if it was not for the love of her foster p
body: 'I entered foster care at 14 and it saved my life'Image caption, Amy Burns says she would not be here today if it was not for the love of her foster parentsByWest of England political editorA woman who entered care at 14 says her foster parents gave her stability, love and a future she never thought possible.The number of foster carers has fallen by 12% since 2021 while the number of children needing care continues to rise.The government has initiated a campaign to get 10,000 more foster care places. Ministers are promoting regional fostering hubs set up in recent years, including in the South West."Fostering definitely saved my life. If I wasn't fostered I don't know who I'd have ended up with," said Amy Burns, who was there for the launch at Downing Street.Amy, now 26, and from Bristol, entered foster care at the age of 14 after what she describes as a difficult family situation.Looking back, she believes the support and stability she received changed the course of her life."I had come out of a really bad family relationship, and if I hadn't been actually saved by my foster parents, I don't know where I'd have ended up."If they didn't stick it out, and if they didn't give me the love that I needed then I absolutely would not be here today."Amy went on to attend university and build a career in the media, something she says would not have been possible without her foster family.Growing demandAmy's story comes as foster carer numbers fall and demand for placements grows. The number of children in care in Bristol and Somerset has risen by 35% over the past seven years.Experts say foster care often delivers better outcomes for children, but a shortage of carers means more young people are ending up in children's homes.Image caption, Amy spoke at an event at Downing Street to launch a new fostering initiative by the governmentAmy was among the speakers at the launch of a new government initiative aimed at recruiting thousands more foster carers.The campaign includes a push to attract people from a wider range of backgrounds and encourage more flexible forms of fostering.Children and Families Minister Josh MacAlister said more people may now be able to consider fostering."Families can come forward in their 20s or 30s or 40s, who might be able to foster part-time at the weekends," he said."Now is the time to come forward and join fostering, because it is changing and it is improving."Guidelines will be made clearer, helped by £88m of new funding.'People talk themselves out of fostering'Also backing the campaign is Wes, a single parent from Yate in South Gloucestershire, who has fostered and adopted children over the past 14 years.Wes, 46, believes many people rule themselves out before finding out what fostering involves."I feel that every day I've made a chance for a child to have a better life," he said.He said concerns about finances or the challenges children may bring should not necessarily stop people from applying."Yes there is trauma, and yes sometimes I have to talk about the past, but to me it's all about the day that you're in and what's coming forward, that child knows that they're going to be safe and happy in my care."Image caption, Wes says fostering can be challenging but also hugely rewardingAmong those supporting recruitment efforts is Jon Hubbard, Wiltshire Council's cabinet member for children's services.His council plays a leading role in the South West Fostering Hub, which was set up two years ago to help councils work together on recruitment and support for foster carers.He said the shortage of foster homes had practical as well as financial consequences because more children end up in residential care, where placements can be significantly more expensive - at £318,000 per year."I cannot stress enough: every foster carer we recruit not only makes a massive difference to a young person's life, but also actually saves a considerable amount of money," he said.Follow BBC Bristol on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to us on email or via WhatsApp on 0800 313 4630.

schema.headline: 'Fostering saved my life,' says Bristol care leaver
